strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck: visual tokens increase multimodal inference cost substantially. Combining attention-based selection with token merging provides a simple approach that preserves the language-model backbone and supports training-free use.

PruMerge+ demonstrates a useful accuracy–compression tradeoff across six image benchmarks and two model sizes. At the reported 25% token budget, the 7B model achieves 76.8 versus 78.5 on VQAv2 and 64.9 versus 64.3 on MMBench.

Training-free experiments on Video-LLaVA provide encouraging evidence beyond still images. ActivityNet-QA accuracy increases from 45.3 to 48.3 with PruMerge, while performance on the other video benchmarks remains broadly stable.

The sampling and fine-tuning ablations provide useful supporting evidence: training-free TextVQA performance reaches 54.0 versus 47.42 for the strongest reported spatial-sampling configuration. Reused methods and datasets are generally credited, and the appendix appropriately acknowledges compression loss and societal implications.
weaknesses: Comparative evidence does not sufficiently establish the contribution over existing token reduction. Table 4 primarily compares against sequential and uniform sampling, without an adapted ToMe baseline or fixed-budget top-k class-attention selection. A matched-budget uniform baseline for PruMerge+ is particularly important because its improved accuracy accompanies substantially more tokens. These controls, under matched fine-tuning conditions, would clarify the benefits of IQR adaptivity and merging.

The efficiency evidence consists of roofline estimates rather than measured performance (Table 2). End-to-end latency, throughput, and peak memory are not reported, including visual encoding, selection/merging overhead, and autoregressive decoding. PruMerge+ also lacks corresponding efficiency results despite providing the strongest accuracy tradeoff. Furthermore, the precision-dependent 'FLOPs' values require an explicit accounting convention, since quantization alone does not reduce the arithmetic operation count.

The specification of PruMerge+ does not explain its reported token budget. Algorithm 1 adds m uniformly sampled tokens to m selected tokens, implying approximately 11% retention when PruMerge retains 5.5%, rather than the reported 25%. Its subsequent loop and output still reference only m tokens. This discrepancy affects the central accuracy–compression comparison and needs a consistent algorithm and per-benchmark token counts.

Important implementation details remain unresolved. Algorithm 1 excludes the selected center from its neighbors and replaces it with an unnormalized attention-weighted sum, although the surrounding text describes weighted averaging and supplementing the retained token. The neighborhood size k, attention-head aggregation, and LoRA configuration are unspecified. Section 3.3 also references final-layer keys while Algorithm 1 specifies penultimate-layer keys. These ambiguities hinder reproduction of the reported method.

The headline performance-preservation claims overstate the results for aggressive PruMerge compression. In Table 1, the 7B model drops from 78.5 to 72.0 on VQAv2, 85.9 to 76.3 on POPE, and 1510.7 to 1350.3 on MME despite fine-tuning. These can still constitute valuable compression tradeoffs, but the claims should distinguish them from PruMerge+'s milder fourfold compression. Section 4.1's statement that POPE improves is also contradicted by Table 1.
